concepts.hook: *Tilsa* — "the Shuttle" — rises at the thaw, when the mending-thread goes back into nets that hung dry all winter.
*Ommar* — "the Awl" — is drawn out in autumn when the women sew the winter sails, and it is said to pierce the first cloud of the season.
*Kesun* — "the Whetstone" — wears a little thinner every year and rises at the turn of the year, when the knives go out for the seal-hunt.
*Thorna* — "the Gaff" — hangs over the strait in high summer, when the big fish come up and must be hauled over the gunwale before they tear the net.
*Ruskel* — "the Fid" — is the splicing spike that opens a rope so new strands can go in, and it rises at the rope-making festival.
*Mesil* — "the Wick Shears" — cut the lamp back at the end of the dark half so the light can come up clean, and they hang in the sky for one night only.
*Hulun* — "the Crook" — is carried over the spring pastures to turn the goats uphill, and it marks the day the herds are driven to the high ground.
*Tenna* — "the Pouch" — is carried on every journey across the islands, and it rises at the start of the dark half, when the lamps are first struck.
*Sekul* — "the Bailer" — is the gourd scoop that empties the boats after the spring rains, and it rises when the thaw-floods come down the valleys.
*Tovel* — "the Trough" — is filled with split fish and salt in the last weeks of autumn, and it is visible only while the salting lasts.
*Ansu* — "the Oil Jar" — carries seal oil to the midwinter feast, and the tipping of its last drop is what the old women watch for in the sky.
*Mirrak* — "the Water Bag" — is a goatskin bottle slung on the drive to summer pasture, and its stitching is said to show when the road is long.
*Halan* — "the Ferry Sail" — is a small square sail raised for the first crossing of spring, and it is flown low over the sound until the boat has landed.
*Sketa* — "the Single Mitten" — has lost its partner on the ice, and it is kept lit for the child who dropped it until the child is grown.
*Ivru* — "the Hood" — is sewn for a newborn in early spring, and it is the first garment the child wears on the road outside the house.
*Tarun* — "the Oilskin" — is the coat of those who go out for the last boats of autumn, and it hangs on the sky over the harbour until every boat is in.
*Telun* — "the Knot Belt" — carries a knot for each day of the year's labour, and one knot is untied at each festival so that the count can be seen.
*Sirel* — "the Quern" — is the hand-mill that turns all night at midwinter, grinding the oats for the dead, and it is the only star that never seems to stop.
*Hannel* — "the Loom Weight" — hangs from the Lamp Road to keep the sky taut, and it is said that if it ever swings, the sailcloth of the year will tear.
*Ketha* — "the Pot Hook" — rises at the first frost, when the stew-pots come in from the yard and are hung over the fire for the winter.
*Ketun* — "the Runner" — is the curved bone that slides the ice-road at midwinter, and it guides travellers across the frozen strait by night.
*Ulsa* — "the Frame" — is the wooden rack where the fish hang to dry in spring, and its shape is said to be the first map of the islands.

concepts.gloss: The Kite Flown for a Drowned Child
concepts.hook: *Minsa* — "the Child's Kite" — is flown every spring with its string left long on purpose, so the drowned child can find her way home if the wind is kind.
*Halenna* — "the Bride-Kite" — is flown from the bride's house to the groom's across the sound, and its tail is said to make the road the bride will walk.
*Tamsi* — "the Fish Kite" — is a bright red kite with a bell, flown to announce to the whole coast that the fish have come, and it rises as the first boats leave.
*Ránu* — "the Ribbon" — is the long trailing ribbon behind the Sun-Kite, and it is said to reach furthest at midsummer, when the kite is flown highest.
*Kessa* — "the Cut Kite" — had its string bitten through by a gull on the longest day, and it drifts along the Lamp Road still, looking for the hand that let it go.
*Surel* — "the Walker" — is carried across the ice before the travellers, its line marking the safe path, and it is put down when the far shore is reached.
*Ilun* — "the Tally Kite" — is flown at each new moon and drops one knot in the string for every month of the year, so that the count can be checked by the wind.
*Lamet* — "the Name-Kite" — is flown at midsummer for an elder who has gone aloft, and it carries the elder's name on a strip of cloth up the Lamp Road.
